(a)The complaint alleges a hostile work environment, constructive discharge, and retaliation. Defendant, plaintiff’s employer, seeks
plaintiff’s prior employment records. See Queen v. City of Bowling Green, 2017 WL 4355689 (W.D.Ky. 2017).
(b)The complaint alleges an insurance company’s failure to pay long-term disability benefits under a pension plan regulated by the
Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. Plaintiff seeks information about the insurer’s policy and methods used to
determine compensation for the claims specialists who handled plaintiff’s claim and the procedures used to monitor claims payments.
See Curtis v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 2016 WL 687164 (N.D.Tex. 2016).
(c)The complaint alleges that the city and a city police officer violated Fourth Amendment rights by using excessive force when
arresting plaintiff. Defendants seek records of paramedic care provided to the arrestee on the day of the arrest. See Booth v. City of
Dallas, 312 F.R.D. 427 (N.D.Tex. 2015).
4. Even if information is relevant, it is discoverable only if disclosure is proportional to the needs of the case in light of the factors set forth in Rule
26(b)(1). The proportionality factors trace back to the 1983 amendments to the Federal Rules, which, at the time, were regarded by the Reporter to the
Advisory Committee that recommended the change as a “180-degree shift” in discovery philosophy. See Miller, The August 1983 Amendments to the
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 33 (Federal Judicial Center 1984). Amendments adopted in 2006 extended the principle of proportionality to
electronic discovery. See Judicial Conference Committee of the United States, Summary Report of the Judicial Conference Committee on Rules of
Practice and Procedure 30–31 (2005). The 2015 amendment essentially moved the proportionality factors from a separate provision in Rule 26(b) to its
current place.
The Advisory Committee Notes to the 2015 amendment emphasize that the relocation of the proportionality factors to Rule 26(b)(1) “does not

change the existing responsibilities of the court and the parties to consider proportionality, and the change does not place on the party seeking discovery
the burden of addressing all proportionality considerations.” However, an empirical analysis of the courts’ application of proportionality factors during
the period prior to and after the 2015 amendment found that the relocation of the requirement “may have fostered real change”; the study reports that
“parties and courts are applying proportionality more than four times more frequently than before the amendment, and that courts are narrowing
